blocks.prompt: The Boat That Sinks on Purpose
blocks.text: A submarine has big empty rooms inside its walls. They are called ballast tanks. When the crew wants to dive, they open valves and let seawater rush into the tanks. The water is heavy. The submarine gets heavier than the sea around it, so it sinks. When the crew wants to go up, they blow air into the tanks. The air pushes the water back out. The submarine gets light again and rises to the top. Sinking and rising is not magic. It is just water going in and air pushing it out.

blocks.prompt: The Submarine That Listens in the Dark
blocks.text: A submarine cannot use its eyes. Sunlight fades fast in the ocean. Go down a few hundred feet and the water turns black. Even if you built a huge window, there would be nothing to see through it. So a submarine listens instead. Sound is strange underwater. It travels about four times faster in seawater than it does in air, and it carries much further. A submarine has a machine called sonar that catches those sounds. Passive sonar just listens. The crew hears propellers turning, whales calling, and rain hitting the surface far above. Active sonar works the other way. The submarine sends out a pulse of sound, a ping, and waits for the echo to bounce back. If the echo returns quickly, the object is close. If it takes longer, the object is far away. Bats and dolphins found this trick long before people did. There is a catch. A ping tells you where things are, but it also tells everyone else exactly where you are.

answers: deep water is black, so there is nothing to see

a quick echo means close, a slow echo means far away
(inference: the ping tells everyone else where the submarine is)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Buoyancy: the rule Archimedes found
A submarine changes weight, not size
Neutral buoyancy: it just hangs there

The pressure hull is a cylinder for strength

blocks.prompt: Why a Steel Tube Floats
blocks.text: Drop a steel bolt in a bathtub and it sinks. Build a ship out of the same steel and it floats. The difference is not the metal. It is the shape. Over two thousand years ago, a Greek thinker named Archimedes worked out the rule. When an object sits in water, it shoves some water out of the way. If the water it shoves aside weighs more than the object does, the object floats. A steel bolt is small and heavy, so it shoves aside almost nothing. A ship is mostly hollow air, so it shoves aside tons. A submarine plays both sides of that rule. Its size never changes, but its weight does. Flood the ballast tanks and the submarine grows heavier than the water it displaces, so it sinks. Blow the tanks out with compressed air and it grows lighter, so it rises. Skilled crews aim for neutral buoyancy, the balance point where the submarine neither sinks nor climbs, and hangs in the water like a held breath. Fine steering comes from dive planes, small wings on the hull. Moving forward, they bite the water and tilt the boat up or down, the way your flat hand tilts out a car window. Then there is the squeeze. Water is heavy, and every thirty three feet down adds the weight of another whole atmosphere pressing in. That is why the inner pressure hull is a cylinder with rounded ends. A curve spreads a load evenly around itself. A flat wall would buckle.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: In your own words, explain the rule Archimedes worked out.
The passage says a submarine's size never changes but its weight does. Why does that matter?

Why is a flat wall a bad idea deep underwater, when it works fine for a house?
answers: (an object floats if the water it pushes aside weighs more than the object does)
changing weight is what lets it sink and rise without changing shape
the balance point where it neither sinks nor rises; it can hang at one depth quietly
(inference: pressure pushes in from every side, and a curve spreads that load while a flat wall buckles)

notes: Early subs ran on batteries and had to surface
USS Nautilus, 1954, first nuclear submarine
1958: it sailed under the North Pole ice

Scrubbers pull carbon dioxide out of the air

blocks.prompt: The Longest Breath
blocks.text: Before 1954, a submarine was not really an underwater boat. It was a surface boat that could hide for a while. Diesel engines burn air, and there is no air to burn under the sea, so those submarines ran on batteries once they dove. Batteries run down. Every day or so the boat had to come up, run its diesels, and recharge. Historians often call those early boats submersibles rather than true submarines, because the ocean always sent them back to the surface. The USS Nautilus changed the argument in 1954. It carried a nuclear reactor, and a reactor does not need air. It splits atoms, boils water into steam, and drives a turbine, and it will keep doing that for years without refueling. In 1958 the Nautilus crossed from the Pacific to the Atlantic underneath the polar ice cap, passing beneath the North Pole with the frozen ocean sealed above its head. Nothing had ever done that before. Endless power buys everything else. Run electricity through seawater and it splits into hydrogen and oxygen. The submarine keeps the oxygen for the crew and pumps the hydrogen over the side. Chemical scrubbers pull the carbon dioxide back out of the breathed air. Other machines boil seawater and condense the steam into fresh drinking water. A modern nuclear submarine makes its own air and its own water out of the ocean it is hiding in. So what stops it? Food. A submarine can only carry so many boxes of it. Crews stack cans in the passageways at the start of a patrol and walk on the floor again weeks later, as the pile shrinks under their boots. There is also the crew itself. Three months in a steel tube with no sunlight, no weather, and no sky is hard on people in ways a reactor never notices. That is the honest answer to how long a submarine can stay down. The machine could go for years. The humans inside it cannot.

6.title: The Boat That Sinks on Purpose
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Boat That Sinks on Purpose

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Seawater absorbs light and radio almost at once
Sound moves about 1,500 meters per second down there
The deep sound channel carries noise for thousands of miles
Anechoic rubber tiles swallow incoming pings
Cavitation: collapsing bubbles make a propeller roar
Trieste, 1960: nearly 11,000 meters down

blocks.prompt: The Ocean Only Speaks One Language
blocks.text: The ocean is a terrible place to be a machine that wants to know things. Almost every tool humans use to sense the world at a distance stops working within a few dozen feet of the surface. Start with light. Seawater eats it. Red vanishes in the first fifteen feet or so, then orange, then yellow. By six hundred feet the world is a dim blue, and below about three thousand feet there is no sunlight at all, ever, anywhere. Windows are pointless. A searchlight buys you a few dozen feet of murk and announces your position to anyone watching. Radio is worse. Radio waves are how the rest of the modern world talks, and saltwater conducts electricity, which means it absorbs them almost on contact. An ordinary radio signal dies within a few feet of the surface. Very low frequency waves push down perhaps twenty meters, which is why a submarine must climb back toward the light to hear from home. Extremely low frequency waves reach deeper, but they crawl, and sending a single short sentence can take several minutes. Navies built ground antennas dozens of miles long to transmit a message roughly the length of a text. That leaves sound, and sound is magnificent down there. In seawater it moves at about fifteen hundred meters per second, more than four times its speed in air, and it does not fade the way light does. Roughly a kilometer down there is a layer where temperature and pressure balance in a way that bends stray sound rays back inward instead of letting them escape. Noise that enters that channel can travel for thousands of miles. Whales appear to have been using it far longer than we have. So a submarine gives up seeing and commits entirely to hearing. Passive sonar is simply listening: hydrophones set along the hull, and a long tail of them towed out behind, feeding the sea to people and computers who can tell a fishing trawler from a warship by the rhythm of its propeller. Every ship has a voice, and navies keep libraries of them. Active sonar, the famous ping, is the option of last resort. It works, and it is honest about it. The pulse goes out, the echo comes back, and you learn where the other object is. So does the other object. Pinging in a hostile ocean is like shouting your name in a dark room full of people you were trying to avoid. This is why a modern submarine is designed, above everything else, to be quiet. Its hull is wrapped in rubber anechoic tiles full of tiny voids that swallow incoming pings and muffle the noise leaking out. Its engines and pumps sit on flexible rafts so their vibration never reaches the steel skin. Its propeller is shaped carefully and turned slowly to prevent cavitation, the collapse of tiny bubbles that makes a fast blade roar. A submarine that can be heard has already lost, so it spends its entire existence trying not to make a sound. And then there is pressure, which listens to nothing. Every ten meters of depth adds roughly one more atmosphere pressing inward. In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the floor of the Challenger Deep, close to eleven thousand meters down, where the water pushes with over a thousand atmospheres, about eight tons on every square inch. On the way down a window cracked and the whole vessel shuddered. They kept going, sat on the bottom for about twenty minutes, and watched the silt they had stirred hang in the dark. The ocean does not care what we would prefer to use. It permits sound. Everything else it swallows.
